book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook starts with 'a derivative is a contract whose value depends on an underlying asset', lists forwards, futures, options and swaps, and treats hedging as one use. Here the narrator starts with his own new shoes and a temple token, lets the learner feel that the token's value moves with the shoes (5000, then 15000) and only then says 'derivative' and 'underlying asset'. Futures arrive as the answer to a felt problem (a crying man who can only buy after 30 days while a banner says prices will rise), the obligation and the buyer's motive come after the deal, and the hedging use is acted out on a real share before the word 'hedging' is said in the last minute. Story and term order is right for beginners; the cost is that options, promised in the title, are left out, and the private one-to-one deal is called a futures contract without saying how exchange futures differ.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Each idea is first lived as a small scene with numbers (my shoes, my token, his salary, my shares), then named, then given its general form; the abstract word always comes after the learner has seen it happen.

opening.what: The narrator shows his new shoes and says the whole topic (derivatives, futures, options, then the stock market and hedging) will be learned from these shoes; promises an eye-opening video.

narration.density: About 14 terms (derivative, underlying asset, bonds, stocks, gold, commodity, forex, financial instrument, futures, options, futures agreement, contractual obligation, sell order, square off, net profit, hedging) in about 9 minutes, about 1.5 per minute. Light on terms but fast in speech (about 210 words per minute); five of the nine minutes go to the shoe story, so the stock-hedging numbers come quickly and the rising case is the hardest stretch.

talmel_summary: In the shoe story the picture does what the voice says: the shoes go into the rack and a token comes back, the token's value is struck and rewritten with the shoe's price, cash and token cross the deal band and both people get ticks; terms land within half a second of their words. In the stock part each number is drawn on the price path or the actor it belongs to, though the picture often runs 1-2 s ahead of the number being said and one written number (+289.85) differs from the spoken 289.95. Weak: about 57 s (215-272) of new ideas over a still band, a 22 s stretch (476-498) with no recognised speech exactly where the futures are closed at 700 (the picture alone shows that step; no tile falls inside the gap), and the fence meaning of hedging only as a caption under a promo overlay.

voice.notes: Fast and chatty, about 210 words per minute, first-person storyteller ('maine', 'mujhe'); dialogue lines are acted with short replies ('nahi nahi', 'mujhe koi problem nahi'). Numbers are read in full rupees, decimals as 'point nine five'; a few numbers are slurred into odd forms in the transcript (5000-500 for 5500). Stress falls on 'derivative', 'contractual obligation', 'mental peace' and 'profit ke liye nahi'. 'Aap kahoge' voices the learner. One speech slip or recognition error: the futures sell price is said as 598.95 in the rising case. No long pauses except the 22 s stretch at 476 s that the recogniser could not read.

game_ideas.player_does: Plays the buyer whose salary comes in 30 days. A banner warns prices may rise. The player either waits or signs a contract with the shoe owner at a chosen price (5200, 5500, 6000), then the 30-day price is drawn (5100, 6000, 8000 or 10000).
game_ideas.process_happens: The contract document drops between the two, cash and token cross the band on day 30, and a meter shows what the player paid against the market price; a 'peace' meter stays full for the contract holder while it swings for the waiter.
game_ideas.win: Can always buy the shoes on day 30 and the price paid never exceeds the budget.
game_ideas.lose: Waiting and drawing 8000 or 10000 leaves the player unable to buy (the crying scene returns); signing and drawing 5100 shows the 400 paid for certainty, so the learner sees a hedge has a cost.
game_ideas.concept: futures agreement: price and date fixed today, both sides bound

game_ideas.player_does: Holds 100 shares bought at 584 of a generic company with bad news on the ticker; decides whether to sell month-end futures at 590, then watches the price path play to the expiry date; may also choose to close the futures early.
game_ideas.process_happens: Two bars move together: share profit/loss and futures profit/loss, with a net bar between them; on the expiry date the futures price meets the share price and the position is squared off.
game_ideas.win: Hedged to expiry, the net bar stays near the locked value whether the path ends at 300 or 984.
game_ideas.lose: Unhedged, the falling path shows a 284-per-share loss; closing the futures early and then seeing the price fall back shows that lifting a hedge is a bet, not hedging.
game_ideas.concept: hedging a share with a futures sell: rising case and closing the futures early

game_ideas.player_does: Matches each derivative card (temple token, gold futures, a currency contract, a share futures) to its underlying asset (shoes, gold, dollars, shares) and then changes the asset's price with a slider.
game_ideas.process_happens: The matched card's value moves with the asset's price, struck and rewritten like the token.
game_ideas.win: All pairs matched so every derivative's value follows its slider.
game_ideas.lose: A wrong pair shows a derivative whose value does not move when 'its' asset moves, which breaks the definition.
game_ideas.concept: underlying assets and derivatives as financial instruments

checks_learned: Every number written on screen must equal the spoken number (screen +289.85 vs spoken 289.95; spoken 598.95 vs screen 589.95), and every written sum must add up (-284 + 289.85 is not 5.95).
A narration stretch over 10 s with no recognised words must be flagged; if a step happens on screen inside it (futures closed at 700), its reason must be re-recorded or written into the script.

A claim like 'profit in both cases' must be checked against the mechanism: a held hedge locks the price, so any gain beyond that must come from a named choice (closing early) that carries its own risk.
A private one-to-one deal used to explain futures must be labelled a forward, with one line on what makes futures different (exchange, standard lots, daily settlement).
Titles and tree branches that promise a topic (options) must either be taught or marked 'next video' on screen.
Spell-check every on-screen title and label (DERIVATES).
No canvas may stay still for more than about 45 s while the narration introduces new ideas (215-272 s here).
A spoken what-if with its own numbers (price only 5100, buyer loses) gets its own picture, not only a sentence.
Real companies, real people, real controversies and broker app screens are replaced with generic ones before BIE uses an example.

teaching_best.why: A temple shoe token is a thing every Indian learner has held; its value moving with the shoes (5000, 15000) teaches 'derivative' and 'underlying asset' before either word is said.
The futures contract enters as the fix for a felt problem: a crying man, a banner, a salary 30 days away; the dialogue keeps it human.
The learner's objection is voiced ('my gain is clear, what does he gain?') and answered with risk and mental peace, so the buyer's motive is learned, not only the mechanics.
The loss case (price only 5100) is admitted, which teaches that a hedge is bought for certainty, not profit.
Both legs of the hedge are worked with numbers and closed with the comparison that matters: +5.95 with the hedge against -284 without it.

teaching_weak.why: The futures are closed at 700 in a stretch the recogniser could not read, and the rising case then claims profit in both cases; as taught, an early exit on a news guess looks like a property of hedging.
A private deal between two people at a temple is called a futures agreement; it is a forward contract, and exchange futures are never contrasted.
Options are named and promised in the title but never taught; the learner is left with half the classification.
The practical example uses a real company, a real person and a live controversy, which dates the lesson and is not neutral; BIE uses a generic company.
No recap: the shoe story, the two stock cases and the hedging name are not tied together at the end.
